Proton. A positively charged subatomic particle and one of the two main constituents of the atomic nucleus. It is a baryon composed of three quarks—two up quarks and one down quark—and is extraordinarily stable. Protons have never been observed to decay, and the number of protons in an atom defines its chemical identity and atomic number.

The proton carries a positive electric charge equal and opposite to the electron's negative charge. It is composed of quarks bound by the strong nuclear force and classified as a baryon. The proton is nearly 1,836 times more massive than an electron, yet vastly smaller. It is the nucleus of a hydrogen atom—the simplest and most abundant element in the universe. Protons are stable over cosmic timescales. Proton decay, if it occurs at all, has an upper limit of ten to the thirty-fourth years. When a proton encounters its antimatter counterpart, an antiproton, both annihilate into pure energy. Protons are confined inside nuclei by the strong force, which increases in strength with distance. The proton's stability underlies atomic matter itself. Without protons, chemistry and complex structures would be impossible. In particle accelerators, protons collide at near-light speed to unlock signatures of exotic particles and test fundamental theories. The proton-to-electron mass ratio of approximately 1,836 is a dimensionless fundamental constant whose origin remains a deep question in physics. Protons belong to the baryon class of particles and are the fundamental constituents made of up and down quarks, clustered in the dense nucleus at an atom's core.
